units.translation: You will say that the ship-fenced host was turned. In both places I have restored the old Attic form ναύφαρκτος [ship-fenced], about which I have spoken in my Oxford notes on Aristophanes' Acharnians 95.
to be young, to grow young
to be young, to grow young
Improperly Ag. 763: But old hubris loves to beget young hubris.
Let him look upon mortal hubris, how it flourishes young (Schnetzius: with what sort of) a root, blooming because of my marriage.
a newly captured antelope that feeds on lion's pasture
and grant that the lovely young women may have lives that bear men
The Youths (title of a play by Aeschylus)
was the title of a play by Aeschylus (fr. 145-148).
neither a great one nor any of the young ones
having sacrificed a perfect victim upon the young ones
Corruptly 766: then or then, when the lordly wrath of light comes young, where H. L. Ahrens in Philologus Suppl. vol. 1 p. 555 reads μόλη φάος τόκου [may the light of birth come].
he has escaped and gone like a fawn
like a dog we track the fawn ––
as double wolves carry a fawn
For other examples see the Thesaurus, vol. 5 p. 1402.
This contest has not come without thought of ancient strife (thus Heath for νίκης [victory]) long ago.
such as are the marks of a victory not shameful, where Hermann reads νείκης [of strife].
How then do these quarrels of the two kings end? (thus Wecklein for βασιλέων [of kings])
and may no strife arise for the city from things unhoped for and unforeseen
I am gone from this quarrel
but he did not resolve the quarrel by taking silver
scorched by the Nile (i.e. by the Egyptian sun)
scorched by the Nile (i.e. by the Egyptian sun)

I tear my tender cheek scorched by the Nile. "Schol.: the one harvested in the Nile, that is, harmed in Egypt; the metaphor is from ears of corn. Wrongly: for it is said rather, like εἰληθερής [sun-warmed], so that it means scorched by the Egyptian sun. The conjectures εἰλοθερῆ [sun-warmed] or Νειλοθαλῆ [Nile-blooming], which the interpreters proposed, seem superfluous since the words with νιλο are better attested." L. Dindorf in the Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 1404.
the Nile sends forth its holy, drinkable stream,
at the very mouth of the Nile, 852 the wide-flowing Nile.
and neighboring the springs of the Egyptian Nile
from the fine-sanded mouths of the Nile
the Nile would nurture such a plant
for the Nile does not nourish a race like that of Inachus
the water of the Nile, untouched by diseases
I worship the divinities around the Nile
and let us no longer honor the outpourings of the Nile with hymns
of the Ethiopian land, where the seven-streamed Nile rolls the earth with a rainstorm of winds
